reveal.title: Jar with dragon
facts: Imperial kilns of Jingdezhen, Jiangxi province
Porcelain painted with cobalt blue under transparent glaze
The Met, Gift of Robert E. Tod, 1937 (37.191.1)
story: This jar comes from the short reign of the Xuande emperor, when the imperial kilns at Jingdezhen made some of the finest blue-and-white porcelain ever fired.

The deep, slightly speckled blue is cobalt brushed onto the raw clay, likely imported from the Middle East, then sealed under a clear glaze. The dragon twisting through clouds was an emblem of the emperor, and the small line of characters near the rim is the reign mark.

reveal.title: Tunic
facts: The Met, Gift of George D. Pratt, 1933 (33.149.100)
story: Cloth was among the most valued things in the Inca world, traded, taxed and given as a reward. This tunic was woven from alpaca or llama fibre and cotton in the Chuquibamba style of southern Peru.

Its grid of eight-pointed stars and small stylized figures repeats across the whole garment. It was made in the final decades of the Inca Empire, just before and after the Spanish arrived in the 1530s.

reveal.title: Pendant mask of Ìyọ́bà Idià
facts: Ivory, iron, brass, coal, traces of iron oxides
The Met, Michael C. Rockefeller Memorial Collection, Gift of Nelson A. Rockefeller, 1972 (1978.412.323)
story: This ivory face portrays Idia, mother of Oba Esigie, who ruled the kingdom of Benin in the early 1500s. She is remembered for raising an army and helping her son win his wars, and he created the title of Queen Mother in her honour.

The Oba wore pendants like this at his hip during ceremonies. Around the crown, carved heads of Portuguese traders alternate with mudfish, linking the king's wealth from overseas trade with Olokun, god of the sea. The two bars on the forehead were once inlaid with iron.

reveal.title: Dagger with Scabbard
facts: Steel, iron, gold, rubies, emeralds, glass, wood, textile
The Met, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund and The Vincent Astor Foundation Gift, 1984 (1984.332)
story: This dagger was made during the reign of Jahangir, the fourth Mughal emperor, whose court ruled much of the Indian subcontinent from cities like Agra and Lahore.

Its gold hilt is set with rubies and emeralds in flowering vines. Daggers like this were less for fighting than for display: emperors gave them to nobles as marks of favour, and courtiers wore them tucked into their sashes.

reveal.title: Cuneiform tablet: private letter
facts: The Met, Gift of Mr. and Mrs. J. J. Klejman, 1966 (66.245.8)
story: Nearly 4,000 years ago, merchants from Assur, a city on the Tigris in what is now Iraq, ran a trading colony at Kanesh, in central Turkey. They brought tin and woollen textiles by donkey caravan and sent home silver and gold.

Tens of thousands of their letters have been dug up at Kültepe. This small palm-sized tablet is one of them: a private letter written in cuneiform, the wedge-shaped script pressed into wet clay with a reed.

reveal.title: Hippopotamus ("William")
facts: Meir, Middle Egypt (tomb of the steward Senbi)
The Met, Gift of Edward S. Harkness, 1917 (17.9.1)
story: Hippos were among the most dangerous animals on the Nile. Placed in a tomb, this one stood for the marshes of the afterlife, with lotus flowers and water plants painted across its body.
Its legs were broken, probably on purpose, so it could not harm the dead man it was buried with. Today it is the unofficial mascot of The Met, nicknamed William.

reveal.title: Terracotta Panathenaic prize amphora
story: Every four years Athens held the Great Panathenaia, a festival for the goddess Athena. Winners did not get medals: they got jars like this filled with olive oil from Athena's sacred trees, sometimes dozens at a time.

By the 300s BCE the old black-figure style was long out of fashion, but prize jars kept it on purpose, as a tradition. This one shows a footrace, and names the official who held office that year, which dates it exactly.

reveal.title: "Gould" Violin
facts: The Met, Gift of George Gould, 1955 (55.86a–c)
story: Antonio Stradivari worked in Cremona, a small city in northern Italy that had been the home of great violin makers since the Amati family in the 1500s.

He made this violin in 1693, during years when he was experimenting with a longer body shape. Like most old violins it was later refitted with a longer neck for modern playing. It is named after the Gould family, who gave it to The Met.

reveal.title: Moon jar
facts: Probably the royal kilns at Gwangju, near Seoul
The Met, Harry G. C. Packard Collection of Asian Art, 1975 (1979.413.1)
story: Jars like this were too big to throw on the wheel in one go, so potters made two deep bowls and joined them rim to rim. That is why the body leans slightly and has a faint line around its middle.
Koreans call them moon jars because the round, milky shape looks like a full moon. Their plainness was the point: the Joseon court valued simple, undecorated white porcelain as a Confucian ideal.

reveal.title: Standing female figure
facts: The Met, Gift of Joanne and Andrall Pearson, 2018 (2018.443.2)
story: In West Mexico, families buried their dead in chambers at the bottom of shafts cut deep into the rock. Hollow clay figures like this one went in with them, often in male and female pairs.

She wears a striped headband, rows of earrings, a nose ring and a wrapped skirt, and her face and shoulders are painted. These details give a rare picture of how people dressed nearly 2,000 years ago.

reveal.title: Armour (Rokumai-dō gusoku) with box
facts: Iron, leather, lacquer, textile, wood, bear fur
The Met, Gift of Rosemarie and Leighton R. Longhi, 2023 (2023.735.1a–o)
story: A gusoku is a full suit of samurai armour, from the helmet and face mask down to the shin guards. This one's cuirass is built from six plates, which is what rokumai-dō means.

By 1689 Japan had been at peace for most of a century. Armour like this was still made with care, but it was worn mostly for ceremonies and processions, and kept in its box as a sign of a family's rank.

reveal.title: Sankofa bird gold weight
facts: The Met, Gift of Ernst Anspach, 1994 (1994.312.16)
story: In the Akan states, including the Asante empire, gold dust was money. Traders weighed it on small scales against brass weights like this one, and every household that traded kept a set.
Many weights illustrate proverbs. This is the sankofa bird, which looks backwards: it stands for the saying that it is no shame to go back and fetch what you forgot, or to learn from the past.

reveal.title: Rolltop desk
facts: Oak, cherry, pine and mahogany, veneered with maple, burl, holly and other woods; mother-of-pearl; leather; gilt bronze
story: David Roentgen ran his workshop in Neuwied, on the Rhine, and sold furniture to Louis XVI, Catherine the Great and other rulers across Europe. His desks were known for hidden drawers and mechanisms.
The pictures on this desk are not painted. They are marquetry: hundreds of pieces of differently coloured and shaded wood fitted together into Chinese-style scenes, a fashion of the time.

reveal.title: Ci wara headdress
story: Among the Bamana of Mali, Ci wara is the being who taught people how to farm. Young men honoured him by dancing in headdresses like this one, tied to a cap and worn with a long fibre costume.

The dancers performed in the fields, often as a male and female pair, to praise the best farmers. Among the Bamana, carvings like this were made by blacksmiths, who also forged the hoes used in the fields.

reveal.title: Robe
facts: The Met, Gift of The Arthur and Madeleine Lejwa Collection, 1975 (1975.388.1)
story: Ikat cloth is made by tying off bundles of thread and dyeing them, again and again, before anything is woven. When the threads go onto the loom the pattern appears, with its soft, feathered edges.
In the oasis cities of Central Asia, like Bukhara and Samarkand, these bold silk robes were worn in layers and given as gifts of honour. The blurred designs were called abr, meaning cloud.
